LESSON 1 OF 106·Cyber Security Fundamentals

What Is Cyber Security?

Security is decisions about what you cannot afford to lose, not a product you install. Start with a bakery, then apply the same four words to your own accounts.

Beginner4 min
Why this matters

Security is not a product you install. It is a set of decisions about what you cannot afford to lose, and what you are willing to do about it. Almost everything else in this course is a detail of those decisions.

What you'll learn

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • explain what security is protecting, in your own words
  • apply the four questions that every security decision comes back to
  • tell the difference between a bug and a security problem

In plain English

Imagine a small bakery. It depends on three things: the recipes that make its bread, the list of customers who order every week, and the card machine that takes payment.

Any of those three can fail. A rival could copy the recipes. A customer list could end up somewhere public. The card machine could be down on the busiest morning of the week.

Security is the work of noticing those three things, deciding what would be worst, and doing something sensible about it before it happens. Nothing about that definition requires a computer. Computers simply make it faster, bigger and harder to see.

How it works

Every security situation, from a bakery to a bank, can be described with the same four words. You will meet them again in lesson four, but they are worth hearing now because they organise everything.

  • An asset is something you would be upset to lose: data, money, a laptop, the ability to take payment.
  • A threat is whatever could take it from you: an attacker, a mistake, a fire, a failing disk.
  • A vulnerability is the gap that lets the threat succeed: a shared password, an unpatched server, a door that does not lock.
  • A control is the specific thing you do about it: encryption, a backup, a lock, a rule.

Security work is a loop over those four words. Decide what matters. Ask what could go wrong. Put a control in place. Then check that the control still works — because the last step is the one everyone skips, and it is the only one that catches a control that quietly stopped working.

A worked example

Take the bakery and run the loop over it. Each line is one decision, and each decision is small enough to actually make.

  • Customer list → a former employee still has access → the shared drive is open to anyone with the link → remove the ex-employee's access and stop using link sharing.
  • Card machine → the provider has an outage → nothing on our side can fix it → keep a manual card terminal and write down what to do during an outage.
  • Recipes → a competitor copies them → they sit in an unlocked drawer → lock the drawer, and keep the digital copies in one folder with restricted access.

Notice that none of those fixes is dramatic, and none of them is a product you buy. That is what most real security looks like.

The mistake most beginners make

People start with the tool instead of the asset. They buy antivirus, or a firewall, or a password manager, and only afterwards wonder what it was supposed to protect.

The other common mistake is the sentence "we have nothing worth stealing". Almost every organisation has a customer list, an email account, or a payment method — and all three are worth money to somebody, which is exactly how automated attacks find them.

Try it in two minutes

Write down five things you would genuinely hate to lose — think about your own accounts, not a company's. For each one, answer two questions:

  • If this disappeared today, what would actually happen this week?
  • If it were copied or seen by someone else, would I know?

If the answer to the second question is "no", you have found the thing to work on first. Not the most valuable asset — the one you would not notice losing.

Practice / apply

You do not need a lab for this lesson. Open a notes app and write the five things you would most hate to lose, then work through the Try it section. Everything stays on your device.

Key takeaways

  • Security is decisions about assets, not a product you install.
  • Asset, threat, vulnerability, control — every situation fits those four words.
  • The loop ends with verification, and verification is the step most people skip.
  • Start from what you would hate to lose, and from what you would not notice losing.
